title: Why optimizing for system comprehension is key to implementing AI for software development

segments.text: Good morning, everybody. My name is Peter Caron. I'm the CEO of 3T Software Labs based here in Berlin. We build software solutions primarily for
database documents document databases like MongoDB, etc. And if you're interested, on the other side of this wall is our stand. You can come over
after the talk and have a talk with us. Welcome to the the third day of We Are Developers. And this morning, I'd like to talk to you a little bit about uh the
concept of developers. What is a developer? And uh when we say we are developers, uh what does it actually mean? Some of you may remember the very first
line, the opening line of the Agile Manifesto written in 2001 was, "We are uncovering better ways of developing software." Better ways does not mean
just making the existing tasks faster or more efficient. And what's happening in the world in the past couple of years with the introduction of AI agents into
the software development life cycle is that software development as a practice is changing. And I'm going to walk you through that uh today. And the definition of what a
developer is. I will go and I'll I'll even say that we are developers will not mean the same thing in 2 years. It will not mean the same thing in 1
year. What is a developer? Better ways does not imply fixing existing workflows. It requires a rethink of workflows. In order to explain this, I want to put
this in a a bit of a context. And uh with me here because this is, I think, extremely important to how we define ourselves as software
development engineers, database engineers, et cetera. What we are talking about is how systems work. And you can look at how systems work in one of uh of two ways in
general. One is as a task-centric view, and the other is as a system-centric view. A task-centric view sees roles like a developer, a software engineer,
as a bundle of tasks. I uh define what I'm going to build, I write a piece of code, I test the code, I deploy the code. Over-simplification
of a bundle of tasks. A system-centric view, on the other hand, is looking at the system in which a workflow or organizational paradigm actually functions.
And this will become uh clear as we move along. So, bundled tasks are not a role. Your role as a software developer or a
product manager or any other function within the software development life cycle is not defined as simply a bundle of tasks. If if we say
that our work is a bundle of tasks, and we use tools, AI can replace each of those tasks. But it can't necessarily replace the
function, the workflow, in which we actually operate. So, the challenge is for us not to confuse a role, software developer, with a bundle of tasks.
I'm going to step back a little bit into what for me is the recent past, but looking at the age of some of the people
in here, maybe it's it's the distant past of ancient Rome or something. Typewriters. Some of you may remember and others may have heard your
grandparents talk about, used to be something called a typing pool. A typing pool was a group of people well, a typing pool was a group of people,
often women, but not entirely, who sat in a room, literally, and typed out documents for people. So, I as a manager or a leader of some sort would write out on
a piece of paper what I wanted to say to a customer or client. I would send that piece of paper down to the typing pool.
A typist would type that, send it back to me for corrections. I would make the corrections on it and I would send that back to the typing pool
to have it typed out. She She would then send it off to the mail room where it would be put in an envelope and and
mailed off. So, in fact, typing pools were an example of a system in which the technology, the workflow, was designed around a particular limited set
of technologies, a typewriter. The pool typist was a role. Typing today is a task. And AIs are really good at typing. But we all know that development,
software development, is not about the typing. It's not typing code. AI is really fast at typing code, but that's not really what the core is.
In the typing pool, a typist would do revision, they would do formatting, error correction, input, all of those things. All of those things that are done by
word processor. And And lo and behold, typists disappeared in the 1980s and 1990s, but typing did not disappear. Now, I choose that example rather than
an example like a switchboard operator or um an ice delivery person. Uh Anybody in the room remember milkmen? When a milkman would come around to the
house and deliver milk to you? Uh has anybody ever seen one of those in the last 20 years? 30 years? 40 years? Oh, somebody
actually You must live in a very rural area right? Yeah, England. Okay. M- You My point exactly. So, a role unbundled is what happens when you take away the
tasks from a particular role. That role ceases to exist. There's no such thing anymore as a typing pool or a typist in a typing pool. But, typing didn't go
away. The task is still there, but the workflow changed, and it changed dramatically. This is what's going to happen in our industry. This is what's already
happening in our industry. I would venture to say that most software developers spend very little time nowadays actually typing code. Um a colleague of mine said to me the other
day when I was bragging about um a a piece of software that I had wrote. He said, "Did you write it or Claude write
it?" It's an interesting question because in fact, I consider what I got the tool to do to be my work. Is it? I don't know. We're going to end up uh
arguing about that in philosophy courses for the next 20 years. But, the fact is is that the AI couldn't come up with the idea by itself to write a proxy to sit
between a client and a DB because it doesn't have the business sense that I do or that I think I do. AI is replacing tasks today.
This is very important, I guess, in this conference. In the very name, we are developers. AI is replacing only the tasks that developers do. It's not actually going
to replace developers. So, when I ask when I say that AI is replacing tasks today, um I don't think it's actually going to replace developers tomorrow.
But, it's not going to not replace developers as we know them today. It's going to replace developers as they were yesterday, as they were last year.
That's true. Developers, however, are going to need to to change. AI may, counterintuitively, like many technologies in the past, actually lead to an increase in the number of people
working with software in the software development life cycle. However, those will not be Rust developers or Go developers or or God help us React
developers. So, what do we do with this? We have to develop strategies for AI software development or software development that incorporates AI. And if we look at this in terms of
task change versus system change, we would optimize existing tasks if we were only interested in task change. So, you make your AI, your Claude, your Copilot write code faster.
You make it respond to prompts easier. That's a task-based change. If we anticipate new tasks on top of existing workflows, and if you if you
walk out and listen to a lot of the talks here, you'll see that the vast majority of people are still talking about how their tools can fit into your
existing workflows. And I think in a transition period, that's probably important, but in the long run, that's just not going to work. You're not going to be able to stuff the
square peg of software development with AI into the round hole of Jira. I I hope there's nobody from Atlassian here. If, however, you switch to a
system-based change or system-based thinking, you alter the logic of value creation. You alter it into new workflows. Different people will be overseeing workflows and decision-making. Now,
uh let me let me just say here, we've already seen this number three here. Alter the logic of value creation, different people overseeing development.
The receptionist, or heaven help us, HR, has come up with a brand new product that they developed over the weekend with their five-year-old child using
um lovable or uh something, and they've come up with a brand new uh um solution. That may or may not work. It may or may
not be valuable in the future. However, we're seeing different people step into different roles. So, where does that leave the developer? The developer is going to have to rethink
where he or she fits into this new workflow. First of all, you have to know what the new workflow is, and then you have to reconceptualize your own
position within in workflow. It's going to be very difficult for individual developers to to deal with this change because what's going to happen is
the technical leaders who run organizations are going to have to have this epiphany first. Uh for the for the past year or so I've

understand about developers. If you read the newspapers, you'll see 8,000 developers let go by uh Meta, 12,000 developers let go by Amazon because inside that the technical
inside those organizations the technical leaders believe that they can replace individuals, individual developers with AI. Meaning an AI agent taking over the role of a
software developer. When in reality, AI agents only take over the some of the tasks of a developer. So what do you what do you do about
this? Uh in the 1990s, there was a woman named Donella Meadows who wrote uh a book called Thinking in Systems. And uh recently there was a book uh by
uh Sajith Paul uh Chudarie called Reshuffle, which I would strongly recommend to to people to read. In this, they describe the the systemic thinking versus
um thinking in terms of tasks and how this impacts negatively transformations. Um the future of software and database development is not far off from what we've already been
doing well at least the best developers have been doing well in software development. So, overseeing the production of maintainable code. David Farley defines good code as code that's easy to
change. This is absolutely true. AI however sometimes ends up creating software that's very difficult or code that's very difficult to change. And what happens is
the best engineers end up being what are called slop janitors and they end up having to fix all of the slop that gets produced by AI. So, we
need to make sure that we oversee the software development done by AI agents um as maintainable code, quality code, maintainable code. We have to manage outcomes because every
AI hallucination hallucination story ends up with the same punchline. The AI did something completely out of context, something that a human would have never even thought to
to do and they'll produce that. We have to manage the outcomes. Humans are really good at seeing large outcome-oriented pictures. That's going to be a key task in the future of
of engineering. We have to control the change. No runaway agents and we have to manage the risk. That means and when I give the example earlier of
of a proxy for MongoDB, you don't necessarily want your database engineers seeing personal data inside your databases. You definitely don't want your AI agents seeing personal PII
data inside your databases. If you don't stop and think about those workflows early, what will happen is that your AI agents will be asked by
somebody, "Oh, please go ahead and identify all the PII data in my database." Well, that really defeats the whole purpose because it's now sitting
somewhere inside the context of the AI. So, protecting it and managing risk is going to be extremely important. The job of the engineer, of the software developer, of the
database developer is going to shift from doing the work to actually governing the work and managing how it gets done. Donella Meadows called these inflection
points. Identifying in a workflow, what are the inflection points? The points where a software developer or a database developer will have to intervene at some
point to redirect AI agents, to reformulate the questions, or to redirect the outcome into what you actually wanted. Now, that is again coordination and oversight.
The receptionist or the HR manager could do that, but they're not well placed to actually make those decisions inside an organization. Software engineers, the
best ones, are. And in the future, that's the role that they will probably be taking. New tasks, not coding, but new tasks in making decisions in how
to move things forward. So, engineering roles, very simply, will integrate AI agents into existing workflows if you don't know what you're doing. AI agents into existing workflows will
create slop faster. You need to let AI coordinate between tasks because it's good at task replication, and you have to learn to create the new
workflows. Assigning product operations now the task of finding and exploiting leverage points that are described by Donella Meadows in these newer workflows is going to be
critical. And here comes something I think I want to take a moment just to describe. The separation between a software developer and a product owner is going
to disappear. Product owners are going to get more and more involved in actually creating code by working inside those at those inflection points, and software developers have to
get a lot better at understanding product. In other words, the outcome. Software developers need to understand the business reasons that they're building software. Now, we could have
said that 5 years ago, and many of us did say that 5 years ago, but not everybody actually followed through and listened. We need to bundle the old engineering
tasks into new roles. Will there be a software engineer in 2 years? Don't know. We are developers may actually change its name from We Are
Developers to something else because a developer will have changed its function. And we need to expect engineers to spend far more time doing product-like things
and managing outcomes. So, rethinking the AI-first organization. Traditional players are going to use AI to optimize existing workflows, and they will get short-term gains,
no doubt about it. But those those organizations that are firing software engineers on a massive scale are going to run into a big difficulty.
People often assume that their jobs are safe because the tasks involved seem resistant to automation. This is the flip side of that coin. However, if we look beyond beyond
individual tasks and consider a broader system that makes that role unnecessary, think back to the typist. We think back that we need to find a
role that won't vanish, that's a pipe dream. We need to adapt our roles to a new reality and a new reality based on AI
being able to replace tasks and tools easier than we can, and then shifting the role of software development engineers, database engineers into making the decisions about what those AI
agents are doing. The coordination can fall to AI. The work can fall to AI, but the direction, the coordination, the outcomes have to remain in the hands of
database developers, software developers, software engineers, and that is what we're going to have to reorient ourselves toward in the future. So, thank you very much for your
